extracted.intended_audience: The people/citizens of New York and readers interested in U.S. constitutional design and the proper structure of executive power (general public, legislators, constitutional framers).
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and design principles for constituting an energetic, independent, and effective executive in a constitutional republic (unity, term length, pay, powers such as veto and military command, judicial separation, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: UNITY of the executive — a single chief magistrate rather than a plural council is a principal distinguishing feature of a good constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single executive produces decision, activity, secrecy, and dispatch; avoids the dilution of responsibility and the cloak of collective councils that may hide faults. Plural councils risk expense (salaries, residence), inefficiency, and can become instruments or accomplices of bad intentions. Examples/comparisons: New York (no council except for appointments) vs. New Jersey (council whose resolutions do not bind).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration in Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration in office is the second requisite to the energy of the Executive: longer tenure increases the probability of firmness and independence in exercising constitutional powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human nature implies greater attachment and willingness to risk for what is held by a durable title. Short tenure tends to produce feebleness, irresolution, and dependence on transient majorities; limited but sufficient duration (e.g., four years is argued as materially contributory) allows the chief magistrate time to establish reputation and act with firmness without unduly endangering public liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from Legislative Influence (via term length and re-eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Term length and the possibility of re-eligibility help secure the Executive's independence from the legislature and popular caprice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Executive must frequently seek continuation by popular or legislative favor, his wishes and fears will tend to corrupt integrity. A fixed duration with the possibility of re-eligibility gives time for administration to establish merit and for the people to retain beneficial leaders. Conversely, exclusion (temporary or perpetual) weakens incentives for good conduct and can diminish independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Exclusion / Support for Re-eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules excluding a chief magistrate from re-eligibility (temporary or permanent) are generally harmful to the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion reduces inducements to good behavior, tempts peculation and usurpation (since rewards are transient), deprives the state of accumulated experience, can remove critical capability in emergencies, and produces mutability of administration and measures. The advantages claimed for exclusion (greater independence, security) are deemed speculative and outweighed by practical harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate Provision for Support (Compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate, fixed compensation for the Executive, not subject to increase or diminution during the term, is essential to preserve independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the legislature can alter salary or provide other emoluments, it gains influence over the Executive (either by starving or buying him). The Constitution's provision that the President 'shall, at stated times, receive for his services a compensation which shall neither be increased nor diminished during the period for which he shall have been elected; and he shall not receive within that period any other emolument' prevents pecuniary intimidation or corruption by the legislature or the states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified Negative (Veto Power) as a Defensive and Deliberative Check
rubrics_metrics.description: A qualified negative (power to return bills with objections, subject to override by a supermajority) is a necessary competent power for the Executive to defend against legislative encroachment and to help prevent bad laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The veto serves both as a shield for the Executive against usurpation by the legislature and as a check to increase deliberation and avoid factional or precipitous legislation. A qualified negative (return for reconsideration with a two‑thirds override) balances being usable without appearing as harsh as an absolute negative, is more likely to be exercised cautiously, and can restrain the passage of bad laws while accepting that it might occasionally block good ones. Historical analogues: the revisionary council in the State (governor with chancellor and judges) has used a qualified negative with perceived success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent Powers (including military command)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive must be vested with competent powers necessary for administration; specifically, command of the armed forces is appropriately placed in the chief magistrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administration includes conduct of foreign negotiations, finance planning, disbursement of public monies, arrangement of forces, and direction of war. The direction of war demands qualities best exercised by a single hand (decision, unity of command). Competent powers are required so the Executive can effectively defend his constitutional sphere and carry out executive functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Independence and Separation from Executive Functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges should be kept distinct from executive avocations; associating judges with executive revisionary or advisory roles risks biasing their interpretation of the law and creating dangerous combinations of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two reasons argued for not using judges as frequent executive associates: (1) prior opinions in revisionary capacities might improperly bias judges who must later interpret the law; (2) frequent association with the Executive could induce judges to embark in the political views of the magistrate, creating a dangerous fusion of executive and judicial authority. It is 'impossible to keep the judges too distinct' from other occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of Administration and Continuity of Measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Stability in the system of administration—continuity of personnel and measures—is an object of executive design and is promoted by sufficient term length and re-eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent turnover in the chief magistrate tends to reverse and undo predecessors' measures, promoting mutability in administration and policy. Stability permits the maturation of plans and preserves experience; enabling the people to continue a useful officer preserves continuity of effective measures and avoids 'disgraceful and ruinous mutability.'
